seoTitle: How to Add Images to a Microsoft Loop Page (2026)
metaDescription: Insert images into a Microsoft Loop page by slash command, drag-and-drop, paste, or web link, resize them, and caption them — plus the one layout limit Loop doesn't advertise.
intro:
Text-only Loop pages get hard to scan once you're documenting mockups, screenshots, or anything visual. A wall of bullet points forces the reader to picture what you mean; a well-placed image settles it in a glance. This guide covers inserting an image into a Loop page from your own files or a web link, resizing it, and captioning it so the context survives after the page has been edited a dozen more times by someone else.

One constraint worth planning around: Loop doesn't let an image sit inline next to text yet, so every image lands on its own line no matter how you insert it.

steps.heading: Open the page you want to add images to
steps.body: Loop's left sidebar lists your pages under Sorted by hierarchy. Loop project, Meeting Notes, and Project Planning sit side by side there, and clicking any one opens it in the main canvas on the right. A new page starts blank, with an Add icon and Add cover prompt above the title and a plain Just start typing... placeholder below it. That placeholder is where the image work happens. If you don't have a page for this yet, use Create new page at the bottom of the sidebar, or start from a built-in template like Project Brief or Meeting Notes instead of a blank canvas.

image.caption: The Loop workspace sidebar and a blank page canvas, with Add icon and Add cover options above the title and a template picker along the bottom.

steps.heading: Insert an image: slash command, drag-and-drop, or paste
steps.body:
Click an empty line where the image should sit, after a heading or between two paragraphs, then type a forward slash to open Loop's command menu. Typing image or media narrows the list to the media block; selecting it swaps that line for an empty upload container. This is the same slash-command pattern Loop uses for headings and tables, so once you've used it here you'll recognize it everywhere else in the app.

Two faster alternatives skip the menu entirely. Drag an image file straight from your desktop or file manager onto the page, or copy a screenshot and paste it in with Ctrl+V (Cmd+V on Mac). Both drop the image onto its own line, exactly the way the slash command does. Loop doesn't currently support placing an image inline next to running text, whichever method you use.

steps.heading: Upload a file, or link to one already online
steps.body:
Choosing the local upload option inside the media block opens your operating system's standard file picker, the same Open dialog you'd see in any other application. Navigate to Downloads, Pictures, or wherever the file lives, then double-click it or select it and hit Open. Loop accepts common formats such as JPEG, PNG, and GIF, and the moment you confirm the selection, the file uploads and renders in place of the empty container.

If the image already lives online (a screenshot on SharePoint, or a graphic from a shared drive link), you don't need to download it first. Paste the direct image URL into the same media block instead, and Loop fetches and renders it, provided the link points straight to an image file and isn't sitting behind a login. That path is faster for anything already shared with your team. It also means the image depends on that external link staying live, so a local upload is the safer choice for anything you can't afford to lose.

image.caption: The standard Windows file picker opened from inside Loop's media block, browsing a Downloads folder for an image to upload.

steps.heading: Resize the image
steps.body: Click the inserted image to select it; handles appear along its edges. Dragging a side handle scales the image's width, and Loop reflows the surrounding blocks automatically, so there's no separate step to fix the layout afterward. A narrower width reads better when the image sits between two paragraphs of explanatory text. Let it run full width when it's the main focus of that section, such as a large mockup or a full-screen capture.

steps.heading: Add a caption
steps.body: Click just below the image to add a short caption line. Describe what the image shows in one plain sentence instead of repeating the paragraph around it. This matters more than it looks on a collaborative page: Loop pages get edited by several people over time, and a caption is often the only thing still explaining an image's purpose after the surrounding paragraph has been rewritten twice. A caption also works as basic alt text, giving the image some descriptive value for anyone using a screen reader.

troubleshooting.problem: The image won't sit next to my text no matter what I try
troubleshooting.cause: Loop doesn't support inline images yet. Every insertion method (slash command, drag-and-drop, or paste) places the image on its own line.
troubleshooting.fix: Design the section with the image as its own block above or below the related text, instead of trying to wrap text around it.

troubleshooting.problem: Pasting an image URL does nothing
troubleshooting.cause: The link doesn't point directly to an image file, or the host requires a login to view it.
troubleshooting.fix: Use a direct link that ends in an image file, or upload the file locally instead.

faq.question: Can I paste a copied image directly onto a Loop page?
faq.answer: Yes. Copy an image or take a screenshot, then press Ctrl+V (Cmd+V on Mac) with your cursor on the page. Loop also accepts a file dragged straight from your desktop or file manager, in addition to the slash-command upload.

faq.question: Why won't my image sit beside my text?
faq.answer: Loop doesn't currently support inline images. Every insertion method drops the image onto its own line, so plan the layout as stacked blocks instead of side-by-side columns.

faq.question: Why isn't my image showing up after I paste a link?
faq.answer: Make sure the URL points directly to an image file and is publicly accessible. A broken link or one that requires sign-in won't render a preview.

faq.question: What image formats does Loop accept for local uploads?
faq.answer: Common formats such as JPEG, PNG, and GIF upload without any conversion, selected through your operating system's standard file picker.

verifiedNote: Click path and screens come from a walkthrough recorded in July 2025. Microsoft doesn't publish a dedicated help article for adding images to a Loop page, so the insertion methods, the on-its-own-line limitation, and the accepted formats were cross-checked against Microsoft's own Loop support page and its Q&A threads on this exact question in September 2026. That check added the paste and drag-and-drop methods and the inline-image limitation, neither of which the previous version of this guide mentioned.
